project.topic: What if a penny doubled every day for 30 days?
project.title: What if a penny doubled every day for 30 days?
project.audience: International, curious nontechnical viewers of science shorts (13+).
project.core_question: If you took one penny that doubles every day for 30 days instead of a million dollars, what would you actually end up with?
project.viewer_takeaway: Doubling looks like nothing for weeks, then explodes: a penny doubled daily is still under $82 after two weeks but passes $1 million on day 28 and ends at $5,368,709.12, half of it added on the very last day, and as real pennies it weighs 1,342 tonnes.

scientific_model.baseline_reality: A US cent weighs 2.5 g and is 19.05 mm across and 1.52 mm thick; $1,000,000 in $100 bills is 10,000 notes of about 1 g each.
scientific_model.counterfactual_change: You refuse $1,000,000 and take one cent that doubles at the start of each day for 30 days (day 1 = 1 cent, day n = 2^(n-1) cents), as physical pennies piling up in your house. Nothing else changes.
assumptions: Day 1 holds one cent; each later day doubles it.
Loose pennies fill about 60% of their heap volume and pile at about 24 degrees.
The house is a small one-storey home with a timber floor over a crawlspace.
The kitchen, the table, the house and the street are illustrative.
causal_chain: After two weeks it is only $81.92.
By day 19 its 655 kg outweighs a horse and breaks the table.
Day 20 is over a tonne yet worth only $5,242.88.
Day 23 is 10.5 tonnes, far beyond a floor’s design load, and goes through it.
Days 29-30 overfill and burst the house.
Day 30 alone adds half of the $5,368,709.12 total.
The refused million would have weighed about 10 kg.
uncertainties: Exactly when a table or floor fails depends on its build; the film shows plausible failures well past design loads.
Heap volume depends on how coins pack (about 50-70%); the house fill dates shift by under a day.
Real pennies of earlier years (pre-1982) weigh 3.11 g.

claims.statement: Starting at one cent and doubling daily gives 2^(n-1) cents on day n: $81.92 on day 14 and $5,368,709.12 on day 30.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Exact figures on the HUD; "eighty-one dollars" spoken.

claims.statement: A US cent minted since 1982 weighs 2.5 g and measures 19.05 mm across and 1.52 mm thick.
Day 19’s 262,144 pennies weigh about 655 kg, more than a typical saddle horse (about 510 kg).
claims.reasoning: 262,144 x 2.5 g; horse weights from University of Minnesota data and the 1,000 lb rule of thumb.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Outweighs a horse" (a typical riding horse, not a draft horse).

claims.statement: A 655 kg pile concentrated on a kitchen tabletop is several times the roughly 1,000 N (about 100 kg) vertical static load used to test domestic tables, so the table would very likely fail.
claims.reasoning: EN 12521 test value from a manufacturer compliance sheet; actual failure load depends on construction.

claims.statement: Day 20’s 524,288 pennies weigh 1.31 tonnes but are worth only $5,242.88.
claims.reasoning: 524,288 pennies at 2.5 g each; 524,288 cents in dollars.

claims.statement: Day 23’s 10.5 tonnes of pennies (about 3 m³ loose) spread over roughly 11 m² is about 900 kg per square metre, and far more under the peak, several times the 40 psf (about 195 kg/m²) design live load for US residential floors, so a timber floor would likely give way.
claims.reasoning: IRC Table R301.5 live loads; heap geometry from the packing and slope assumptions.
claims.presentation_guardrail: Illustrative failure of a suspended timber floor.

claims.statement: At about 60% packing, day 28’s pennies take about 97 m³, day 29’s about 194 m³ and day 30’s about 390 m³, so a small one-storey house (about 180 m³ inside, crawlspace included) is full on day 29 and overflowing on day 30.
claims.reasoning: Coin bounding volume 0.433 cm³ divided by the packing fraction; house volume from its dimensions.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Burst out of your house" for days 29-30.

claims.statement: Each doubling adds as much as everything before it, so day 30 adds $2,684,354.56, half of the final $5,368,709.12.
claims.presentation_guardrail: "Half of it arrived on the last day."

claims.statement: A US banknote weighs about 1 gram, so $1,000,000 in $100 bills (10,000 notes, 100 bundles) weighs about 10 kg and fits in a briefcase, against 1,342 tonnes of pennies.
claims.reasoning: US Currency Education Program: about 1 g per note; bundle size 156 × 66 mm.

creative_direction.logline: You turn down a million dollars for a penny that doubles every day: for weeks it is pocket change, then it breaks your table, sinks through your floor, passes the million on day 28 and bursts your house, half of it arriving on the very last day.
creative_direction.visual_identity: Warm morning kitchen at eye level with an elegant boxless money counter in the top-left; true-size copper coins that hop out of their twins; a heap that cracks the table and the floor; a suburban house bursting with copper; a gold x-ray of the last day.
creative_direction.lighting: Morning sun through the kitchen window with a warm pendant lamp; outdoors, morning sun from the front right.
creative_direction.camera_language: Eye-level POV that leans in to one penny, pulls back as it multiplies, steps back as furniture and floor fail; across-the-street handheld for the house; a crane over the mound; a tilt from the briefcase to the mound.
creative_direction.motion_language: Comic, physical doubling: coins pop out of twins, pours land each day, wood cracks, boards drop, walls fall outward one after another.
creative_direction.world_scale_policy: True metre scale throughout; coins at true size; heap volumes from coin counts.
creative_direction.opening_hook: You just turned down one million dollars for a single penny.
creative_direction.mid_video_rehook: Day 20 is over a tonne of pennies that has already broken your table, yet it is worth only $5,242.88, so the million still looks smarter until the floor goes and day 28 finally passes it.
creative_direction.ending_payoff: The million you refused would have fit in a briefcase.
creative_direction.loop_connection: The briefcase that leaves in the first seconds returns, open, beside the mound in the last shot.
creative_direction.asset_policy: Reuse the room kit, village houses, trees, sky rig and HUD; add a reusable coin-pile-v1 (true-size coins, volume-derived heap, twin hops and pours).

audio.voice_style: Crisp, urgent, fascinated adult male; high-tension simulation narrator; brisk opening cadence
audio.music_direction: Original light score: a plucked, curious figure that speeds up with the doubling, a held breath before each failure, a bright chord when the million is passed, a shimmering swell for the x-ray, and a small button at the end.
audio.sfx_direction: Coin clinks that double into a cascade; the briefcase clack; wood cracking; floorboards and joists breaking in sequence; window glass bursting; walls falling one after another; a copper avalanche; silence drops before the table, floor and house fail.
